question: What is a bean definition in Spring?
title: Spring Bean Definition Explained
direct_answer: A **bean definition** is the metadata Spring uses to create a bean: the class type, scope (singleton/prototype), constructor args, property values, init/destroy methods, and lifecycle callbacks. Spring stores bean definitions in the `BeanFactory` and creates instances from them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring's internal bean metadata model
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing bean definition (metadata) with bean instance (the actual object)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the distinction between bean definition (blueprint) and bean instance (the object)

sections.title: Bean Definition vs Bean Instance
sections.content:
A **bean definition** is the blueprint — metadata describing how to create a bean. A **bean instance** is the actual object Spring creates from that blueprint. Think of it like a class definition vs an object instance. The bean definition specifies:
- **Class**: which Java class to instantiate
- **Scope**: singleton (one shared instance) or prototype (new instance each time)
- **Constructor arguments**: for constructor injection
- **Properties**: for setter injection
- **Init/destroy methods**: lifecycle callbacks
- **Lazy**: whether to create eagerly or on first request

sections.title: How to Define Beans
sections.content:
Three ways to create a bean definition:
1. **`@Component`** (and variants) — Spring creates definition via component scanning
2. **`@Bean` in `@Configuration`** — explicit bean factory method
3. **XML** — `<bean class="com.example.UserService">` (legacy)

Bean definition metadata includes: class, scope, init-method, destroy-method, lazy-init, autowire mode

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A bean definition is essentially the blueprint that Spring uses to create and configure a bean. It contains information like which class to instantiate, what scope to use (singleton or prototype), what constructor arguments to pass, and what lifecycle methods to call. When Spring starts up, it reads all the annotations and configuration and builds a registry of bean definitions. Then it creates actual bean instances from those definitions. The distinction matters because there's always exactly one bean definition per bean type, but there could be multiple instances if the scope is prototype.

seo.metaTitle: Spring Bean Definition Explained | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn what a Spring bean definition is, the metadata it contains, and the difference between a bean definition (blueprint) and a bean instance.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Spring reads your class like a blueprint before it ever builds the object — that blueprint is the bean definition.

beats.text: A bean definition is the metadata Spring stores to describe how to create a bean. It's not the bean itself — it's the recipe. It holds the class to instantiate, the scope (singleton or prototype), constructor arguments, properties to inject, and lifecycle method names. Spring reads all your annotations at startup and builds a registry of these definitions before creating any instances.

Separating the blueprint from the object lets Spring manage scope correctly. One definition can produce one singleton instance or hundreds of prototype instances depending on configuration. Without this separation, changing scope would require rewriting the creation logic.

items: Class: which Java class to instantiate — the core of the definition.
Scope: singleton means one shared instance; prototype means a new instance per injection.
Constructor arguments and properties: captured for dependency injection during instantiation.
Init and destroy method names: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy hook into the lifecycle.
Lazy flag: controls whether Spring creates the bean eagerly at startup or waits until first access.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, @Service on UserService causes Spring to register a bean definition: class=UserService, scope=singleton, constructor-arg=UserRepository. Later Spring uses that definition to create one UserService instance and inject it everywhere it's needed. candidates miss: there's always exactly one bean definition per registered bean, but singleton scope means one instance while prototype scope can produce many instances from that same definition.

items: Don't confuse the definition with the instance — asking how many bean definitions exist is different from asking how many bean instances are live.
Bean definitions are frozen after context refresh — you can't add new definitions at runtime in a standard Spring Boot app.

speakable_v2.cap: The bean definition is Spring's recipe card — one recipe, but the number of dishes it produces depends on the scope.
followup_handoff: How does Spring store and retrieve bean definitions internally?
What happens to bean definitions when the ApplicationContext refreshes?

question: What is the @Bean annotation and when do you use it?
title: @Bean Annotation in Spring — Usage and Purpose
direct_answer: **`@Bean`** is a method-level annotation in a `@Configuration` class that declares a bean. The method returns the object to register as a Spring bean. Use it when you can't put `@Component` on a class — typically for third-party library classes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of explicit bean definition for third-party classes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @Bean must be inside a @Configuration class
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give concrete examples of classes you'd register with @Bean: ObjectMapper, RestTemplate, DataSource

sections.title: @Bean Usage Examples
Key Points
sections.content:
- Must be inside a `@Configuration` class
- Method return type determines bean type
- Method name is the default bean name (customizable with `name=`)
- Can have parameters — Spring injects them from the container
- `@Bean` with `@Scope("prototype")` creates new instance per injection
- `@Primary`, `@Lazy`, `@DependsOn` can be combined with `@Bean`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Bean` is used inside a `@Configuration` class to manually define a bean. It's the way to register classes you don't own — third-party library classes where you can't add `@Component`. For example, Jackson's `ObjectMapper`, Spring's `RestTemplate`, or a database `DataSource` — you write a method that creates and configures the object, annotate it with `@Bean`, and Spring registers the return value as a bean. The method name becomes the bean name by default. Method parameters are automatically injected from the container, so you can pass dependencies into the bean you're creating.

followup_questions: What is the bean name when you use @Bean?
What is @Configuration and why is it needed?

seo.metaTitle: @Bean Annotation Spring Usage | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn when and how to use @Bean annotation in Spring @Configuration classes to register third-party library classes as Spring beans.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: You can't add @Component to Jackson's ObjectMapper — @Bean is how you hand Spring a class you don't own.

beats.text: @Bean is a method-level annotation placed inside a @Configuration class. The method creates and returns the object you want Spring to manage. Spring registers the return value as a bean, using the method name as the default bean name. The method can accept parameters — Spring resolves and injects them from the context automatically.

@Component works only when you own the source code and can add annotations. But third-party classes like Jackson's ObjectMapper or a database connection pool don't have @Component on them. @Bean lets you write the creation code yourself and hand the result to Spring.

items: Basic: @Bean on a no-arg method — Spring calls it once and registers the return value.
Named: @Bean(name="myBean") overrides the default method-name-based name.
With parameters: Spring injects each parameter from the context before calling the method.
Combined with @Scope, @Primary, @Lazy, or @DependsOn for advanced lifecycle control.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, AppConfig is a @Configuration class with an objectMapper() method annotated @Bean. Inside, you call new ObjectMapper() and register the JavaTimeModule so Java 8 date types serialize correctly. Spring calls this method once and makes the configured ObjectMapper available for injection anywhere in the app. sharp edge: if you put @Bean in a class annotated only with @Component (not @Configuration), the CGLIB proxy is absent and calling one @Bean method from another will create a new instance each time — breaking singleton semantics.

items: @Bean must live in a class that Spring scans — if the @Configuration class is outside the component scan package, its beans won't be registered.
Avoid business logic inside @Bean methods — keep them as thin factory methods.

speakable_v2.cap: @Bean is your escape hatch for beans you can't annotate directly — use it in @Configuration to register any class as a Spring-managed bean.
followup_handoff: What happens when you call one @Bean method from another inside a @Configuration class?
How do @Bean method parameters get resolved by Spring?

question: What is @Configuration in Spring and how is it different from @Component?
title: @Configuration vs @Component in Spring
direct_answer: **`@Configuration`** marks a class as a source of `@Bean` definitions and ensures Spring proxies the class so `@Bean` methods always return the same singleton instance. **`@Component`** registers the class itself as a bean. `@Configuration` is a specialization of `@Component`.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @Configuration is CGLIB-proxied to enforce singleton semantics for @Bean methods
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the @Configuration CGLIB proxy: calling a @Bean method directly from another method still returns the singleton

sections.title: The @Configuration CGLIB Proxy
Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Configuration` → CGLIB proxy → `@Bean` methods always return singleton
- `@Component` → no proxy → `@Bean` methods create new instance each call
- `@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false)` → disables proxy for performance (Spring Boot 2.2+)
- Use `@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false)` when `@Bean` methods don't call each other
- `@Configuration` is also a `@Component` — it gets detected by component scanning

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The important difference is the proxy behavior. When you use `@Configuration`, Spring wraps the class in a CGLIB proxy. This proxy intercepts calls to `@Bean` methods to ensure they always return the same singleton instance — even if you call the method directly from another `@Bean` method within the same class. Without this, calling `beanC()` directly would create a new object each time, breaking singleton semantics. `@Component` doesn't get this proxy behavior. In Spring Boot 2.2+, if your `@Bean` methods don't call each other, you can use `@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false)` to skip the proxy overhead.

followup_questions: What is CGLIB proxying in Spring?
Can you use @Bean methods in a @Component class?

seo.metaTitle: @Configuration vs @Component Spring | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Understand the difference between @Configuration and @Component in Spring, including CGLIB proxy behavior and singleton semantics for @Bean methods.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Both get picked up by component scanning, but @Configuration gets a superpower: a proxy that guarantees singleton semantics for every @Bean method.

groups.heading: @Configuration
groups.text: Marks a class as a factory for @Bean definitions. Spring wraps it in a CGLIB proxy at startup. When any @Bean method is called — even directly from another @Bean method — the proxy intercepts and returns the existing singleton instead of creating a new object.

groups.heading: @Component
groups.text: Registers the class itself as a bean. No CGLIB proxy. If you put @Bean methods inside a @Component class, calling one @Bean method directly from another will bypass Spring and create a brand new object each time — breaking singletons.

items: Use @Configuration whenever you define @Bean methods — the proxy guarantee is essential for correct singleton behavior.
Use @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false) when your @Bean methods are standalone and never call each other — it's faster to start up.
Use @Component for classes that don't define beans, like services, listeners, and utilities.

beats.text: gotcha: in our Spring Boot 3.2 AppConfig, beanA() calls beanC() directly. With @Configuration, Spring's proxy intercepts that call and returns the same C singleton that beanB() already received. Without the proxy (if you used @Component), A and B would each get a different C instance — subtle bugs with shared state.

speakable_v2.cap: @Configuration is @Component plus a proxy. Use @Configuration for bean factories; use @Component for everything else.
followup_handoff: What is CGLIB and how does Spring use it to proxy @Configuration classes?
When would you use proxyBeanMethods=false and what are the tradeoffs?

question: What is @Lazy in Spring and when would you use it?
title: @Lazy Bean Initialization in Spring
direct_answer: **`@Lazy`** defers bean creation until the bean is first accessed. By default, singleton beans are created at startup (eager). `@Lazy` on a bean or injection point creates the bean on first use. Useful for expensive beans or circular dependency workarounds.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overusing @Lazy — can hide startup errors that eager init catches
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the tradeoff: @Lazy delays errors until runtime instead of surfacing at startup

sections.title: @Lazy vs Eager Initialization
Key Points
sections.content:
- Default: singleton beans are **eagerly** initialized at startup
- `@Lazy` on `@Bean` or `@Component` → created on first access
- `@Lazy` on `@Autowired` injection point → injects a proxy, defers creation
- Use case 1: expensive beans not always needed (heavy ML models, large caches)
- Use case 2: circular dependency workaround (`@Autowired @Lazy BeanB b`)
- Downside: startup errors hidden until runtime
- Spring Boot: `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` — all beans lazy

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Lazy` tells Spring not to create a bean at startup — instead, create it the first time it's actually needed. The main use case is for expensive beans that take a long time to initialize or consume a lot of resources, especially if they're not needed for every request. Another use case is as a workaround for circular dependencies. The downside of lazy initialization is that configuration errors only surface when the bean is first accessed, instead of at startup. For production apps, you generally want errors to surface at startup, so `@Lazy` should be used selectively. Spring Boot does have a `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true` flag that makes everything lazy for faster startup in dev.

followup_questions: What is the difference between lazy and eager bean initialization?
What is the risk of using @Lazy?

seo.metaTitle: @Lazy Bean Initialization Spring | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn what @Lazy does in Spring for deferred bean creation, when to use it for expensive beans, and the tradeoff vs eager initialization.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Faster startup sounds great — but @Lazy trades speed for safety by hiding config errors until someone actually uses the bean.

beats.text: You're optimising for startup time or resource usage. By default, Spring creates all singleton beans eagerly at startup. @Lazy defers creation until first access. This matters for beans that are expensive to initialize — large connection pools, ML models, heavy caches — especially if those beans aren't needed on every request.

items: Eager (default): all singleton beans created at startup. Errors surface immediately. Startup is slower but predictable.
@Lazy on a @Bean or @Component: that specific bean is deferred until first access.
@Lazy on an @Autowired injection point: Spring injects a proxy at startup; the real bean is created on first method call.
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true: makes every bean lazy globally — useful in dev for fast restarts, not for production.

beats.text: Use @Lazy on a specific bean when it's genuinely expensive and not always needed — a report-generation service that's only called once a day, for example. Don't use it broadly in production. production trap: @Lazy on a misconfigured bean means the error doesn't appear until that bean is first requested — possibly hours into a production run.

items: You're adding @Lazy to fix a startup performance problem — profile first to confirm the bean is actually the bottleneck.
You're using @Lazy to work around a circular dependency — that's a workaround, not a fix. Refactor the design instead.

speakable_v2.cap: @Lazy is a targeted tool for genuinely expensive optional beans — don't sprinkle it everywhere hoping for a faster startup.
followup_handoff: How does @Lazy work on an @Autowired injection point — what proxy does Spring inject?
What's the difference between @Lazy and spring.main.lazy-initialization=true?

question: What is @DependsOn in Spring and when do you need it?
title: @DependsOn Bean Ordering in Spring
direct_answer: **`@DependsOn("beanName")`** forces Spring to initialize a named bean before the annotated bean. Use it when one bean has a side effect (like setting up a database schema or initializing a shared resource) that another bean relies on, but there's no direct dependency that Spring can detect.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @DependsOn unnecessarily when a direct @Autowired dependency would handle ordering

sections.title: When @DependsOn Is Needed
Key Points
sections.content:
- Forces initialization order without a direct dependency
- Only needed for **implicit** dependencies (side effects, shared resources)
- For explicit dependencies, just `@Autowired` — Spring handles ordering automatically
- Multiple deps: `@DependsOn({"beanA", "beanB"})`
- `@DependsOn` usage is a design smell — if A really needs B, make it explicit

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@DependsOn` controls bean initialization order when there's an implicit dependency — when one bean needs another's side effects but doesn't directly inject it. The most common scenario is when an initialization bean sets up some shared state (like creating database tables or a cache) that another bean relies on. You'd annotate the dependent bean with `@DependsOn("initializerBeanName")` so Spring initializes the initializer first. In practice, if you find yourself needing `@DependsOn` often, it's worth reconsidering the design — usually the dependency can be made explicit through `@Autowired`, which is cleaner.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @DependsOn and @Autowired for ordering?
When would you use @DependsOn in practice?
How does Spring determine bean initialization order normally?

seo.metaTitle: @DependsOn Spring Bean Ordering | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn when and how to use @DependsOn in Spring to control bean initialization order for implicit dependencies and side effects.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: @DependsOn is for the invisible dependency — when bean B needs bean A to have already run, but doesn't inject A directly.

beats.text: @DependsOn tells Spring to initialize a named bean before the annotated bean, even though there's no direct @Autowired link between them. It's purely an ordering guarantee. Spring normally determines initialization order from its dependency graph — @DependsOn extends that graph with an explicit edge for cases Spring can't infer automatically.

Spring can only detect order dependencies it can see — @Autowired fields and constructor parameters. Implicit side-effect dependencies, like 'bean A must run DDL before bean B reads the tables,' are invisible to Spring. @DependsOn makes them explicit.

items: Single dependency: @DependsOn("beanName") — ensures one named bean initializes first.
Multiple dependencies: @DependsOn({"beanA", "beanB"}) — both must initialize before the annotated bean.
Applicable to @Bean methods and @Component classes alike.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, DatabaseSchemaInitializer runs Flyway migrations at startup. CacheLoader reads from the freshly-migrated tables. CacheLoader doesn't inject DatabaseSchemaInitializer — it just needs the tables to exist. You add @DependsOn("databaseSchemaInitializer") on CacheLoader's @Bean method so Spring guarantees the migration completes first. non-obvious: if CacheLoader did @Autowire DatabaseSchemaInitializer, Spring would already order them correctly — @DependsOn is only needed when the link is invisible.

items: Don't use @DependsOn when a direct @Autowired dependency would do the job — the explicit injection is both cleaner and self-documenting.
Frequent use of @DependsOn is a design smell — it often means initialization logic should be consolidated into one bean.

speakable_v2.cap: @DependsOn is a last resort for side-effect ordering — if you can model the dependency explicitly with @Autowired, do that instead.
followup_handoff: How does Spring build its bean initialization order graph from @Autowired dependencies?
Can @DependsOn cause a deadlock if there's a circular ordering?

question: What is bean naming in Spring and how do you set a custom bean name?
title: Spring Bean Naming Conventions
direct_answer: By default, `@Component`/`@Service` beans are named after the class with a lowercase first letter (`UserService` → `userService`). `@Bean` methods are named after the method. Set custom names with `@Component("myName")`, `@Bean(name="myBean")`, or `@Qualifier("myName")`.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the default naming convention
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when you'd need a custom name: multiple beans of the same type, @Qualifier matching

sections.title: Bean Naming Conventions
Key Points
sections.content:
- Default: class name with lowercase first letter
- `@Bean` default: method name
- Custom: `@Component("name")` or `@Bean(name="name")`
- Multiple names (aliases): `@Bean(name={"name1", "name2"})`
- `@Qualifier` matches by bean name for disambiguation
- `applicationContext.getBean("beanName")` looks up by name

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Spring's default naming convention is to take the class name and lowercase the first letter — so `UserService` becomes `userService` and `OrderRepository` becomes `orderRepository`. For `@Bean` methods, the method name is the bean name. When you need a custom name, you pass the name as a value to the annotation — `@Service("myUserService")` or `@Bean(name="primaryDataSource")`. Custom names matter when you have multiple beans of the same type and need to reference them by name using `@Qualifier`. You can also give a bean multiple names by passing an array to `@Bean(name={...})`.

followup_questions: Can two beans have the same name?
How do you look up a bean by name programmatically?

seo.metaTitle: Spring Bean Naming Conventions | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn Spring bean naming conventions, how default names are derived from class names, and how to set custom names with @Component and @Bean annotations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Spring names your beans for free — but when you have two beans of the same type, knowing those names is the only way to pick the right one.

beats.text: Every Spring bean has a name — a string identifier used to look it up and to match @Qualifier references. By default, @Component and its specializations derive the name from the class name with the first letter lowercased. @Bean methods use the method name. Custom names override the default by passing a string value to the annotation.

Bean names are how you resolve ambiguity. When you have two beans of the same type, type-based injection alone fails. @Qualifier uses the bean name to select the right one. Understanding names is also essential when using applicationContext.getBean() for dynamic lookup.

items: Default for @Service/@Component: class name with lowercase first letter — UserService becomes userService.
Default for @Bean method: method name — public DataSource primaryDataSource() becomes bean name primaryDataSource.
Custom single name: @Component("myBean") or @Bean(name="myBean").
Multiple aliases: @Bean(name={"primaryDs", "mainDs"}) — the bean answers to either name.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, there are two DataSource beans: devDataSource() and prodDataSource(). Their names are devDataSource and prodDataSource by default. You inject the right one with @Qualifier("devDataSource") at the injection point. gotcha: if you rename the method from devDataSource to devDs, the default name changes too — and any @Qualifier("devDataSource") references break silently. Use explicit @Bean(name="devDataSource") to lock the name.

items: Renaming a method that provides a @Bean changes the default bean name — existing @Qualifier references will break.
Two beans can't share the same name in the same context — Spring throws BeanDefinitionOverrideException unless you explicitly allow overriding.

speakable_v2.cap: Know the default naming rule, name your beans explicitly when they'll be referenced by @Qualifier, and never let a method rename silently change a bean name you depend on.
followup_handoff: What happens if two beans have the same name in the same ApplicationContext?
How does applicationContext.getBean(name) differ from type-based injection?
